abstract: The August 2026 revision of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab's 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' study, extending the original August 2025 paper with ADP administrative payroll data through June 2026. Using a balanced panel of firms observed monthly from January 2021, comprising 3.5 to 5 million workers per month, the authors document six descriptive facts about the US labor market after the diffusion of generative AI. The central finding is a divergence by age and AI exposure: aggregate employment continues to grow, but employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations now stands 19 percent below where it would be had it kept pace with their less-exposed peers, while experienced workers show no comparable gap. This revision changes the headline measure. Earlier vintages led with a regression estimate adjusting for firm-level shocks; the authors now emphasize the simpler descriptive kept-pace divergence, which requires no modeling choices. They are explicit that these are early descriptive indicators, not causal estimates, and they publish a companion set of AI Economic Indicators for ongoing tracking.
keyFindings: Fact 1: No evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement. Average employment in the ADP sample rose about 6 percent between November 2022 and June 2026, while employment in the most exposed quintile grew about 4 percent.

Fact 2: Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations stands 19 percent below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers. In levels, the two most exposed quintiles fell about 11 percent between November 2022 and June 2026 while the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10 percent, a divergence of 21 percentage points.

Fact 3: The divergence has widened steadily. By the kept-pace measure the shortfall was 15 percent at the July 2025 data vintage and 19 percent as of June 2026. The prior regression-adjusted headline ran 13 percent (July 2025 data) then 16 percent (September 2025 data).

Fact 4: The decline operates through reduced hiring rather than increased separations. Separation rates fell for both groups and, among young workers, fell at least as much in the most exposed occupations as in the least exposed, the opposite of what displacement would imply.

Fact 5: Declines concentrate where Anthropic Economic Index usage is primarily automative. Occupations with the highest estimated augmentative (complementary) shares show flat or rising employment, and are not ordered by complementarity exposure.

Fact 6: Adjustment is occurring through employment rather than base compensation. Little difference in compensation trends by age or exposure quintile; among job-stayers real base pay grew somewhat more slowly in exposed jobs, small relative to the roughly 20-percentage-point employment divergence.

Occupation-level long-difference regression, workers aged 22 to 25: employment in the most exposed quintile declined about 18 percentage points relative to the least exposed (Table 1 Panel A, -0.179). Adding a college-share control attenuates this to -0.09, still significant at the 10 percent level (Panel C). In the sample balanced since 2021 the range is -0.19 with no controls and -0.06 with college share, the latter no longer significant.

Total employment for 22-to-25-year-olds was roughly flat over the period (a 1.9 percent decline). The two most exposed quintiles were about 57 percent of employment in this age group in November 2022, so their 11 percent decline subtracted about 6 percentage points, most of which growth in less-exposed quintiles offset.
About 60 percent of occupations in the least-exposed quintile saw rising early-career employment over the period, against about 30 percent in the most-exposed quintile.

Dose response by adoption: using state-level relative usage from the Anthropic Economic Index (February 2026 release), the decline for exposed young workers is sharpest in leading-adoption states (about -19 percent for the most exposed quintile) and smallest in emerging-adoption states.

Regional variation: the relative decline appears in every Census region, largest in the West (about -21 percent from the November 2022 level) and Northeast (-13 percent), smallest in the South (-7 percent) and Midwest (-9 percent).

Gender: women work in more AI-exposed occupations than men at every age, in ADP and in the CPS and ACS alike. Declines for young women are steeper than for young men, consistent with greater concentration in declining high-exposure roles.

External validity: on the comparable 2022-to-2024 window the most-versus-least-exposed gap for ages 22 to 25 is -0.022 [-0.055, +0.011] in the ACS against -0.132 in ADP. The ADP gap has since widened to about -0.205 by mid-2026. Within professional, information and financial services the two sources agree closely (-0.231 ADP vs -0.213 [-0.353, -0.072] ACS).
methodology: High-frequency administrative payroll records from ADP, whose clients collectively employ over 26 million US workers. The analysis sample is a balanced panel of firms observed monthly from January 2021 through June 2026, comprising 3.5 to 5 million workers per month. AI exposure is the GPT-4 beta measure of Eloundou et al. (2024), grouped into occupation quintiles, with five alternative exposure measures used for robustness. The headline is a descriptive kept-pace divergence: the shortfall in employment growth for ages 22 to 25 in the most exposed quintiles relative to the growth actually realized by the least exposed quintiles. Supporting estimates are employment-weighted occupation-level long-difference regressions of the percent change in employment between November 2022 and June 2026 on exposure-quintile indicators, with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; Table 1 balances firms since January 2018 (the primary sample, which permits pre-trend assessment) and Table 2 since 2021. Control panels add occupational interest-rate exposure (Zens et al. 2020), college share from the 2017 ACS, the work-from-home measure of Lambert and Schindler (2026), and teleworkability (Dingel and Neiman 2020). Confounding by firm-level shocks is tested with Poisson event-study regressions carrying firm-time and firm-quintile fixed effects. Automation versus augmentation splits use the Anthropic Economic Index (March 2025 release, with September 2025 / January 2026 / April 2026 releases pooled in the appendix). Benchmarks against the CPS and the 2024 ACS appear in Appendix H.
qualifiers: Tier 1: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper on administrative payroll microdata, widely cited but not peer-reviewed. The authors state plainly that these are descriptive facts, not causal estimates, and that ongoing work is needed to determine how much is caused by generative AI rather than merely correlated with it. Three limitations they raise directly. First, more- and less-exposed occupations show divergent trends predating ChatGPT, particularly around the COVID-19 pandemic; the relative gap rose about 13 percentage points from its 2018-2019 baseline to a mid-2020 peak and has since fallen about 30 points, so roughly 13 points unwind the pandemic boom and the remaining 17 carry the gap below baseline. Second, estimates attenuate substantially when controlling for occupational education (-0.179 to -0.09), which may be either an alternative explanation or the very channel through which AI operates, since generative AI substitutes best for the codified knowledge taught through formal schooling; the authors present the two as bracketing a range rather than picking one. Third, the magnitude is more pronounced in ADP than in national survey benchmarks: the ACS gap is -0.022 with a confidence interval including zero against -0.132 in ADP on the comparable window, though the direction is consistent and the two agree closely for white-collar occupations. Restricting the ACS to full-time civilian wage and salary workers moves it only slightly, so coverage differences explain little of the discrepancy; the authors note the 2024 ACS weighting revision as a partial confound and report an unweighted diagnostic that moves the ACS gap to -0.047. Selection in which firms use ADP remains an open concern, as does the possibility that changes within the ADP sample reflect reallocation to firms outside it. Base compensation excludes bonuses, overtime, commissions, equity and tips, precisely the components largest in the most exposed high-income occupations, so Fact 6 cannot rule out unobserved compensation adjustment. This is the third published vintage of the same study on the same panel, so its successive estimates are not independent observations.
